items.name: Academic and research integrity: UGC (Promotion of Academic Integrity and Prevention of Plagiarism in HEIs) Regulations 2018 and ICMJE authorship and AI-use recommendations
items.one_line: For theses, papers and books from Indian HEIs, UGC grades text similarity into penalty levels and requires a signed originality undertaking; for journal articles, ICMJE says authors must meet four criteria, AI cannot be an author, and any AI use must be disclosed.

sources.title: UGC (Promotion of Academic Integrity and Prevention of Plagiarism in Higher Educational Institutions) Regulations, 2018, Gazette of India, 23 July 2018
sources.supports: definition of plagiarism, scope (scripts), originality undertaking, exclusions, similarity levels and penalties

sources.title: ICMJE Recommendations: Defining the Role of Authors and Contributors
sources.supports: four authorship criteria; non-author contributors acknowledged; AI-assisted technology disclosure; chatbots not authors

sources.title: ICMJE Recommendations: Use of AI by Authors
sources.supports: disclose AI use at submission; humans responsible; AI-generated material not acceptable as primary source; nondisclosure may be misconduct

items.note: UGC regulations notified 23 July 2018 (Gazette text read 2026-10-05); ICMJE pages read 2026-10-05. Rules for a writer or editor: (1) UGC defines plagiarism as 'the practice of taking someone else's work or idea and passing them as one's own'; it covers master's and research-level 'scripts' (theses, dissertations, papers, book chapters, books) but excludes 'assignments / term papers / project reports / course work / essays'. (2) Every student submitting a thesis or dissertation signs 'an undertaking indicating that the document has been prepared by him or her and ... is his/her original work and free of any plagiarism', checked with an HEI-approved detection tool; ghostwriting a thesis for a client makes that undertaking false. (3) Similarity levels: 'Level 0: Similarities upto 10%' (no penalty), Level 1 above 10% to 40%, Level 2 above 40% to 60%, Level 3 above 60% (students: revise, debarment, or registration cancelled; for publications: withdraw manuscript and further penalties); quoted work with permission or attribution, references and generic terms are excluded, and core parts (abstract, hypothesis, results, conclusions) 'shall not have any similarities'. (4) ICMJE: an author must meet all four criteria (substantial contribution; drafting or critical review; final approval; agreement to be accountable); others go in acknowledgements. 'Chatbots (such as ChatGPT) should not be listed as authors'; AI writing help is described in the acknowledgements, AI in data or figures in the methods; 'Referencing AI-generated material as the primary source is not acceptable' and 'Nondisclosure of AI use may require corrective action and may be construed as misconduct'. (5) Medical writers who draft for named authors must be acknowledged; unacknowledged ghostwriting conflicts with the contributor rules. Related: comp:us_copyright_ai_authorship, comp:admissions_ai_essay_policies.

items.name: University admissions rules on AI-written and ghostwritten application essays (UCAS personal statement, Common App fraud policy)
items.one_line: UCAS applicants declare their personal statement was not copied or produced by AI and UCAS runs similarity checks; Common App treats submitting AI output or another person's writing as one's own as fraud that can close the account and be reported to every college on the list.

sources.title: UCAS: A guide to using AI and ChatGPT with your personal statement
sources.supports: AI-generated statement could be considered cheating; applicant declaration; Verification Team similarity checks; permitted uses (ideas, structure, checking)

sources.title: Common App: Fraud Policy (accordion text read in a browser pane)
sources.supports: definition of fraud incl. AI output; actions after a fraud determination

items.note: Both pages read 2026-10-05 (Common App text is inside collapsed accordions, read via a browser). Rules for a writer helping an applicant: (1) UCAS: 'Generating (and then copying, pasting and submitting) all or a large part of your personal statement' from an AI tool 'and presenting it as your own words, could be considered cheating by universities and colleges and could affect your chances of an offer'; 'you now have to declare that your personal statement hasn't been copied or provided from another source, including artificial intelligence software'. (2) UCAS's Verification Team 'run checks to detect fraudulent applications and patterns of similarity'; UCAS advises using AI only to 'help you make a start, structure, and then check your final work'. (3) Common App fraud includes 'intentionally misrepresenting as one's own original work ... the substantive content or output of an artificial intelligence platform, technology, or algorithm' (or another person's ideas or language). Consequences may include 'permanent suspension, temporary suspension, or termination of their Common App user account, and disclosure of the Fraud to the Registered User's "My Colleges List."' (4) So a paid SOP / personal-statement service may coach, question, structure and edit the applicant's own material, but must not write the substance or invent experiences; individual universities may add stricter rules, check each one. Related: comp:academic_integrity_ugc_icmje.

items.name: Amazon A+ Content guidelines (KDP public page): prohibited claims, prices, reviews, guarantees and time-sensitive words
items.one_line: A+ Content below an Amazon listing must not carry prices, promotions, 'buy now' calls, customer reviews, guarantees, contact details, competitor mentions, time-sensitive words or unsubstantiated certification, award, '#1/top-rated' or eco claims; violations get the content rejected and can remove the ASIN.

sources.title: Amazon KDP Help: A+ Content Guidelines (public, no login)
sources.supports: top rejection reasons, image and text formatting, claims and awards, content restrictions, consequences

items.note: Read 2026-10-05 on the public KDP help page; the Seller Central (brand) A+ guidelines are behind a seller login and were not read, so treat these as the KDP version and expect the seller version to be at least this strict (secondary seller guides list the same core bans). Rules for a copywriter: (1) No pricing or promotion: 'Do not include pricing, promotional details or discounts', promotional words ("affordable", "bonus", "free") or purchase prompts ("buy now", "add to cart", "get yours now", "shop with us"). (2) No customer reviews ('We don't allow customer reviews in A+ Content'); at most four quotes or endorsements, only from well-known publications or public figures, attributed; no quotes from private individuals. (3) No time-sensitive words: 'now, new, latest, yet, on sale now, the latest product, the best yet, or references to holidays'. (4) Claims: certification claims ('recommended by, certified, tested, approved, proven, validated') and awards need a note naming the body, study or publication and year; no awards older than 2 years; 'Environmental claims with words like "eco-friendly," "biodegradable," and "compostable," including their symbols, are not allowed'; 'recyclable' needs substantiation; satisfaction and boastful claims ('100% satisfaction guaranteed', '#1 rated', 'top-rated') are not allowed. (5) 'Guarantee information, including references to off-Amazon return or refund policies, is strictly forbidden'; no shipping details, QR codes, phone, address or email; no competitor mentions (comparison charts only against your own products); no mimicking Amazon logos or page headings. Consequence: 'rejection by our system, potential removal of your ASIN, or both'. Related: plat:amazon_product_listing, plat:amazon_kdp_book, comp:amazon_in_restricted_products.

items.name: BIS IS 19000:2022 Online Consumer Reviews (India) and the Department of Consumer Affairs framework on fake and deceptive reviews
items.one_line: Indian Standard for any organisation that publishes consumer reviews online: verify the review author, keep a written code of practice, never edit a review to alter its message, never suppress or discourage negative reviews; voluntary when launched, with a mandatory Quality Control Order proposed in 2024.

sources.title: PIB (Dept of Consumer Affairs), 21 Nov 2022: Centre launches framework for safeguarding and protecting consumer interest from fake and deceptive reviews in e-commerce
sources.supports: launch, scope (every online platform publishing consumer reviews), voluntary status, guiding principles, author verification methods, moderation and publication duties

sources.title: PIB (BIS), 12 Dec 2022: BIS issues standards for organizations publishing consumer reviews
sources.supports: applies to sellers collecting reviews from their own customers, contracted third parties and independent third parties

sources.title: PIB (Dept of Consumer Affairs), 15 May 2024: stakeholder consultation on protection of consumers from online fake reviews
sources.supports: draft Quality Control Order: prohibitions on biased collection, editing reviews, discouraging negative reviews

items.note: Status as read 2026-10-05: launched 21 Nov 2022, 'The standard will initially be voluntary for compliance by all e-commerce platform' (PIB 1877733); on 15 May 2024 DoCA consulted on a draft Quality Control Order to make it binding (PIB 2020665); this pass found no notified QCO, so check before calling it mandatory. The standard text itself is a paid BIS document (not read); rules below are from the official press releases. Rules for a copywriter: (1) it covers 'any organization that publishes consumer reviews online, including suppliers/sellers of products and services that collect reviews from their own customers' (PIB 1882828), so a brand's own site testimonials are in scope. (2) Proposed prohibitions: 'The organisation shall not edit reviews to alter their message' and 'shall not prevent or discourage people from submitting negative reviews' (PIB 2020665): never rewrite, polish or cherry-edit a real review you quote. (3) 'shall not publish consumer reviews online collected with a bias objective and prejudice' (PIB 2020665): no review-gating campaigns that only invite happy customers. (4) Review authors are to be verified (email, phone/SMS, link confirmation, captcha) and platforms keep a written code of practice (PIB 1877733): writing reviews for a client under invented names defeats this and, 'once made mandatory', 'may be considered as an unfair trade practice' reportable to the CCPA (PIB 1877733). Related: comp:ccpa_misleading_ads_2022, comp:ftc_consumer_reviews_rule, comp:uk_dmcc_schedule20.

items.name: Companies Act, 2013 section 135 + CSR Policy Rules, 2014: corporate social responsibility (Schedule VII, CSR reporting)
items.one_line: What a company may call CSR in its reports, website and impact stories: only Schedule VII activities under its board-approved policy, never sponsorships for marketing benefit, employee-only perks or political donations.

sources.title: Indian Kanoon: The Companies Act, 2013 (s.135)
sources.supports: s.135 as originally enacted: thresholds, CSR committee, policy disclosure on website, 2% spend, reasons for unspent amount in Board's report (secondary; later amendments not reflected)

sources.title: AUBSP: Companies (CSR Policy) Rules, 2014 as amended (Sept 2022)
sources.supports: secondary reproduction of amended rule 2(1)(d) exclusions, rule 8 impact assessment, rule 9 website disclosure

sources.title: MCA: Instruction Kit for eForm CSR-2
sources.supports: official MCA form for reporting CSR (page refused fetch with 403 on 2026-10-05; known from search listing only)

items.note: In force; s.135 and the CSR Rules were amended in January 2021 (MCA, per search listing of mca.gov.in); primary MCA / India Code pages refused fetch 2026-10-05, so text read from secondary reproductions: medium confidence. For a copywriter writing CSR reports, impact stories, website CSR pages or the CSR annexure: (1) The board-approved CSR Policy must indicate activities 'as specified in Schedule VII', and its contents are disclosed in the Board's report and placed on the company's website (s.135(3)-(4)). (2) The Board must 'mandatorily disclose the composition of the CSR Committee, and CSR Policy and Projects approved by the Board on their website' (CSR Rules r.9, secondary text). (3) Not CSR: activities in the normal course of business; activities outside India (except training Indian sports personnel); any contribution to a political party; activities benefitting the company's own employees; 'activities supported by the companies on sponsorship basis for deriving marketing benefits'; activities done to meet another statutory obligation (r.2(1)(d), secondary text). So a branded sponsorship or a marketing campaign cannot be presented as CSR spend. (4) If the company does not spend its CSR amount, the Board's report must give the reasons (s.135(5)); large-obligation companies must commission an independent impact assessment for big projects (r.8, secondary text). (5) CSR spend is also reported to MCA in eForm CSR-2 (MCA instruction kit). Thresholds, percentages and penalties: quote only from the current India Code text.

items.name: Companies Act, 2013 section 42: private placement of securities (no public advertising)
items.one_line: A company raising money by private placement may only make named offers to a recorded select group and may not advertise or market the offer to the public in any medium.

sources.title: Indian Kanoon: Section 42 in The Companies Act, 2013
sources.supports: current (post-2017 amendment) text of s.42 incl. named offers (sub-s.7) and the ban on public advertisement (sub-s.8); secondary reproduction because India Code and mca.gov.in refused the fetch (403 / no DNS) on 2026-10-05

sources.title: KPMG India: Private placement of securities: need for caution (Jun 2024)
sources.supports: secondary commentary on enforcement of s.42 (not read in full)

items.note: In force (text read on Indian Kanoon 2026-10-05; India Code and MCA pages blocked, so medium confidence). For a copywriter: (1) 'No company ... shall release any public advertisements or utilise any media, marketing or distribution channels or agents to inform the public at large' (s.42(8)): no ads, social posts, influencer pushes, mass emails or landing pages pitching a live private round. (2) Offers go only to persons 'whose names are recorded by the company prior to the invitation', and they 'shall receive the offer by name' (s.42(7)): investor letters are addressed, not broadcast. (3) The offer goes to no more than fifty persons 'or such higher number as may be prescribed' in a financial year (excluding QIBs and ESOP employees); go over and it is 'deemed to be an offer to the public' with full prospectus rules (s.42(2) Explanation I, s.42(4)). (4) Subscription money only by cheque, demand draft or banking channels, never cash (s.42(5)). Copy that announces a round AFTER allotment (a funding-news press release) is outside the ban, but a 'we are raising, invest now' call to the public is not. The prescribed higher number and the penalty are not taken from memory: check the Companies (Prospectus and Allotment of Securities) Rules before quoting.

items.name: Nonprofit fundraising appeals in India: FCRA 2010 (foreign donations) and the income-tax donation deduction (80G under the 1961 Act, s.133 under the Income-tax Act, 2025)
items.one_line: What a donation appeal may promise: foreign money only if the NGO holds FCRA registration and routes it to its SBI New Delhi FCRA account, and a tax-benefit line only if the donee is approved and will file the donation statement and certificate.

sources.title: PIB: Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act: FAQs (22 July 2026)
sources.supports: registration / prior permission, single SBI New Delhi FCRA account, barred recipients, FCRA Amendment Bill 2026 (introduced 25 Mar 2026) and FCRA Amendment Rules notified 22 Jun 2026

sources.title: MHA: FAQs on FCRA
sources.supports: official FAQ (downloaded, not quoted)

sources.title: Income Tax Department: FAQs related to Section 80G (Dec 2025)
sources.supports: cash limit, Form 10BD / 10BE matching, no 80G under the new tax regime

sources.title: Income Tax e-filing: Form 113-114 User Manual
sources.supports: from tax year 2026-27 donees file Form 113 under s.354(1) of the Income-tax Act, 2025 for donations qualifying under s.133(1)(b)(ii); donors get Form 114 certificates

items.note: Status as read 2026-10-05: FCRA 2010 in force; FCRA Amendment Rules notified 22 June 2026; FCRA (Amendment) Bill, 2026 introduced in Lok Sabha 25 March 2026 (PIB FAQ, 22 Jul 2026; check whether it has passed before quoting it). Income-tax Act, 2025 governs from tax year 2026-27 (e-filing Form 113 manual); the 1961 Act's s.80G still applies to earlier years. For a fundraising copywriter: (1) Foreign donations: an association may receive foreign contribution only 'after obtaining registration or prior permission', and 'All foreign contributions must first arrive in a single designated FCRA account at the State Bank of India's New Delhi Main Branch' (PIB FAQ). So an appeal aimed at NRIs holding foreign passports, foreign foundations or overseas crowdfunding must not invite foreign money unless the NGO is FCRA-registered, and it must route that money to the FCRA account, never the domestic account. (2) Political parties, election candidates, legislators, public servants, organisations of a political nature and specified news-media persons and entities cannot receive foreign contribution at all (PIB FAQ, citing section 3). (3) Tax-benefit lines ('save tax', '50% tax exemption under 80G') are true only if the donee holds a current approval (registration number stated) and files the donation statement: 'it is mandatory that the deduction claimed by the donor under Section 80G ... matches with the details submitted by the donee in Form 10BD', and the donor gets a Form 10BE certificate (80G FAQ); from tax year 2026-27 the equivalents are Form 113 (statement) and Form 114 (certificate) under the 2025 Act (e-filing manual). (4) 'No deduction shall be allowed under Section 80G ... exceeding two thousand rupees unless such sum is paid by any mode other than cash' (80G FAQ Q12), and the deduction 'cannot be claimed if you opt for the new tax regime' (Q15): a blanket 'tax-free donation' promise is misleading. (5) Do not state the deduction percentage or limit without checking the donee's category in the current Act. Penalties not taken from memory.

items.name: Food Safety and Standards (Labelling and Display) Regulations, 2020 (FSSAI): veg / non-veg logo, menu calorie display, front-of-pack name
items.one_line: FSSAI rules for food labels and restaurant menus: green-dot / brown-triangle veg and non-veg logo also on leaflets and ads, true name of the food on the front of pack, and calories per serving plus the 2,000 kcal reference line on menus of chains with 10+ outlets or a central licence.

sources.title: FSSAI: Compendium, Food Safety and Standards (Labelling and Display) Regulations, 2020, Version VIII (09.09.2025)
sources.supports: consolidated text: commencement, definitions (Front of Pack), reg 5(1) name of food, 5(4) veg/non-veg symbols and use in advertisements, reg 9 display in food service establishments

items.note: Consolidated text Version VIII dated 09.09.2025 read 2026-10-05; Chapter 3 (food service display) compliance 'w.e.f 1st July, 2022' per the FSSAI direction noted in the compendium. Rules for a copywriter: (1) Veg/non-veg: non-veg = 'a brown colour filled triangle inside a square with brown outline'; veg = 'a green colour filled circle inside a square with green outline' (reg 5(4)(a),(b)); the declaration 'shall also be prominently displayed ... on the pamphlets, leaflets and advertisements in any media' (5(4)(d)), so food ads, menus and delivery-app creatives carry the logo; egg-only products may add an egg declaration next to the symbol. (2) Front of pack must carry the name that shows 'the true nature of the food'; a coined, fanciful or brand name may be added only in compliance with the Advertising and Claims Regulations 2018 (5(1)(c); see comp:fssai_advertising_claims_2018 for nutrition and health claims). (3) Menus: Food Service Establishments 'having Central license or outlets at 10 or more locations shall mention the calorific value (in kcal per serving and serving size)' against menu items and display 'An average active adult requires 2,000 kcal energy per day, however, calorie needs may vary' (reg 9(1)); all FSEs show allergen info (symbols allowed) and the veg/non-veg logo against items (9(2)); event caterers operating under 60 days a year, free self-serve condiments and special-order items are exempt (9(3)). (4) Fuller nutrition info is given on request in booklets, handouts or website, with 'deviation of 25 percent' tolerated (9(4)); e-commerce food platforms must carry the same information (9(5)). (5) No front-of-pack nutrition rating (star rating / HFSS warning) appears in this consolidated text; do not write that one is mandatory. Pan masala packs and their ads carry a warning covering 50% of the front of pack (Schedule).

items.name: FTC Enforcement Policy Statement on Deceptively Formatted Advertisements (2015) and Native Advertising: A Guide for Businesses
items.one_line: US rule for native ads, advertorials and sponsored content: an ad must not look like independent editorial content, and any label must be clear, unambiguous and placed where people look first.

sources.title: FTC: Commission Enforcement Policy Statement on Deceptively Formatted Advertisements (Dec 22, 2015)
sources.supports: full text: deception standard for ad format, net impression, disclosure adequacy

sources.title: FTC: Native Advertising: A Guide for Businesses (Dec 2015)
sources.supports: plain-language guide: acceptable labels, placement, search results, in-feed ads

items.note: Issued 22 Dec 2015 and still on ftc.gov as current guidance (pages read 2026-10-05). For a copywriter: (1) 'The Commission will find an advertisement deceptive if the ad misleads reasonable consumers as to its nature or source' (including who sponsored it), and such ads are deceptive 'even if the product claims communicated are truthful' (Policy Statement). (2) Judged on the net impression of the whole piece (look, style, byline, layout), not one line; an advertorial styled like the host site's news needs a disclosure (Policy Statement). (3) Labels likely understood: 'Ad', 'Advertisement', 'Paid Advertisement', 'Sponsored Advertising Content'; avoid 'Promoted' or 'Promoted Stories', and phrases like 'Presented by', 'Brought to You by', 'Sponsored by [X]' can read as funding only, not authorship (Business Guide). (4) Place the disclosure 'in front of or above the headline', in contrasting text, where consumers look first; in non-paid search results put it at the beginning of the title tag (Business Guide). (5) A disclosure in body text may not cure a misleading headline, because people may glance only at the headline (Policy Statement). Penalty figures not taken from memory.

items.name: Indian crowdfunding platform content rules (Ketto, Milaap): truthful medical and cause fundraiser stories, consent, no manufactured vulnerability
items.one_line: Ketto and Milaap make the campaigner legally responsible for a true, non-misleading story with all material facts disclosed; Ketto also requires consent for every person shown, bans staged distress and AI or digital manipulation that harms authenticity, and limits how children are photographed.

sources.title: Ketto: Terms of Use
sources.supports: campaigner duties (true, not misleading, all material facts), deletion for false info, image consent and authenticity guidelines, child protection, AI manipulation ban

sources.title: Milaap: Terms of Use
sources.supports: no content the user knows is false, misleading or inaccurate; fund-use responsibility; Milaap branding on campaign collaterals

items.note: Both terms read 2026-10-05 (no update date shown on either page). Rules for a fundraiser-appeal writer: (1) Ketto: the campaigner must ensure the campaign description 'is not misleading and describes the need and use of the funds to be raised'; Ketto 'reserves the right to delete your Campaign' if information is 'false, does not depict the true nature of the Campaign or is misleading in any manner'; the campaigner must 'disclose all material facts relating to the beneficiary, purpose and campaign' and update them if they change (e.g. 'change of purpose, death of beneficiary'). So: real diagnosis, real hospital, real amount and what it covers; no invented urgency or inflated figures. (2) Consent: images only 'when you have consent from the people depicted or their parents/guardians'; explain how images and stories will be used; no payment or incentive for consent. (3) Authenticity: 'never use images that make people look more desperate or powerless than they are'; 'Ketto does not encourage manufacturing fake vulnerability for the sake of emotional appeal' (do not make a parent cry or fold hands on camera); 'Manipulation of images in post- production or their alteration/enhancement using artificial intelligence or other digital means is strictly prohibited if it negatively affects image authenticity'; content must not 'portray or focus on ailments or deformities egregiously'. (4) Children: specific nudity limits and no setting up images to make children look more vulnerable (Ketto); a child-sexual-abuse survivor's identity is barred by law (comp:india_sexual_offence_victim_identity). (5) Milaap: users must not submit content they know 'is false, misleading, or inaccurate', the campaigner alone is responsible for using funds for the stated purpose, and campaign marketing collaterals must carry Milaap's logo branding as per its guidelines. Related: comp:dpdp_act_rules (health data of the beneficiary).

items.name: Job ads and hiring copy in India: Code on Wages, 2019 (no gender discrimination in recruitment), RPwD Act, 2016 s.20 and Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019
items.one_line: A job post or careers page may not restrict, prefer or price a role by sex or gender (including transgender identity), and must not screen out transgender candidates or, for government employers, people with disabilities.

sources.title: Ministry of Labour: The Code on Wages, 2019 (Gazette text, No. 29 of 2019)
sources.supports: s.3: no gender discrimination in wages; no discrimination on the ground of sex while recruiting

sources.title: PIB: Code on Wages, 2019 factsheet (23 Nov 2025)
sources.supports: government reading of s.3: no discrimination on the basis of gender, including transgender identity, in recruitment, wages or conditions

sources.title: Indian Kanoon: The Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016
sources.supports: s.20 non-discrimination in employment (Government establishments) and definitions (secondary reproduction)

sources.title: Indian Kanoon: Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019
sources.supports: s.3 prohibition against discrimination incl. employment; s.9 establishments may not discriminate in recruitment (secondary reproduction)

items.note: Status as read 2026-10-05: the four Labour Codes, including the Code on Wages, 2019, were implemented with effect from 21 Nov 2025 (web-search summary of PIB / labour.gov.in pages; the PIB factsheet of 23 Nov 2025 read here does not itself state the date). RPwD Act 2016 and Transgender Persons Act 2019 in force (texts read on Indian Kanoon: medium confidence). For a recruitment or employer-brand copywriter: (1) no employer may 'make any discrimination on the ground of sex while recruiting any employee for the same work or work of similar nature' or in conditions of employment, unless a law restricts women's employment in that work (Code on Wages s.3(2)(ii)); and no gender gap in wages for the same or similar work (s.3(1)). So 'male candidates only', 'female preferred' or a different salary band by gender are out unless a law restricts that role. PIB reads s.3 as covering 'gender, including transgender identity'. (2) 'No establishment shall discriminate against any transgender person in any matter relating to employment including, but not limited to, recruitment, promotion and other related issues' (Transgender Act s.9), and no person or establishment may deny employment or treat a transgender person unfairly in employment (s.3(b)-(c)). (3) 'No Government establishment shall discriminate against any person with disability in any matter relating to employment' (RPwD s.20(1)), must provide 'reasonable accommodation' (s.20(2)), and 'No promotion shall be denied to a person merely on the ground of disability' (s.20(3)). The RPwD duty in s.20 is written for Government establishments (incl. government companies and aided bodies); private employers fall under other RPwD provisions not read here. (4) Write requirements as job-related abilities, not gender, appearance or 'able-bodied' filters. Penalties not quoted from memory. Related: comp:rpwd_act_accessibility (accessibility of the careers page itself).

items.name: Personality and publicity rights in India: Delhi HC and Bombay HC orders protecting a person's name, voice, image and likeness (incl. AI voice clones and deepfakes)
items.one_line: Indian courts restrain commercial use of a well-known person's name, image, voice, catchphrase or AI-cloned likeness without consent, while leaving news, genuine criticism and authentic satire or parody protected; ads and AI content must not borrow a celebrity's persona.

sources.title: Delhi HC, Anil Kapoor v. Simply Life India & Ors, CS(COMM) 652/2023, order of 20 Sep 2023 (Indian Kanoon copy of the digitally signed order)
sources.supports: persona elements protected (name, voice, image, manner of speaking, dialogue, gestures, signature); restraint on AI, deepfake, face-morphing and GIF misuse; free speech carve-out for news, satire, parody and criticism

sources.title: SCC Online blog (secondary): Bombay HC ad-interim injunction for Arijit Singh, 26 Jul 2024
sources.supports: Bombay HC restrains AI voice cloning of a singer's voice and vocal style

sources.title: MediaNama (secondary), Sep 2026: Delhi High Court to define personality rights
sources.supports: Delhi HC hearing (Sep 2026) on the scope of personality rights; list of earlier orders (Amitabh Bachchan 2022, Anil Kapoor 2023, Jackie Shroff 2024, Arijit Singh Bombay HC 2024, Sadhguru 2025); court wary of blanket takedowns

items.note: Judge-made, no statute; read 2026-10-05. The Anil Kapoor order was read in full (Indian Kanoon copy); the Bombay HC and the Sep 2026 hearing come from secondary summaries (named above). Rules for a copywriter: (1) Do not use a well-known person's name, image, voice, catchphrase or style in an ad, product, merchandise or ringtone without written consent: the Delhi HC restrained use of 'name, likeness, image, voice, personality or any other aspects of his persona' 'using technological tools such as Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, deep fakes, face morphing, GIFs either for monetary gains or otherwise' (Anil Kapoor, para 48); a signature phrase can be protected too (that order covered 'Jhakaas', per the case summaries). (2) AI voice clones and sound-alikes are covered: Bombay HC (Arijit Singh, Jul 2024, secondary) and Delhi HC (Kumar Sanu, Oct 2025, secondary) restrained AI tools reproducing a singer's voice and vocal style; never script 'in the voice of [celebrity]' VO or 'AI cover' promos. (3) Editorial use survives: 'free speech in respect of a well-known person is protected ... right to information, news, satire, parody that is authentic, and also genuine criticism', but not once it 'results in tarnishment, blackening' of the persona (Anil Kapoor, para 38). Satire must read as satire and must not sell a product. (4) Implied endorsement is the core harm: no copy may suggest a celebrity endorses, attends, or can be 'booked' via the brand (para 39). (5) The law is moving: a Delhi HC bench was hearing the scope of the right in Sep 2026 (MediaNama, secondary); check before relying on parody or fan-content defences. See also comp:emblems_names_act_1950, comp:amazon_in_restricted_products, comp:it_rules_sgi_2026.

items.name: Professional-body advertising bans in India: Bar Council of India Rule 36 (advocates), ICAI clauses 6-7 and Website Guidelines (chartered accountants), IMC/NMC ethics regulations (doctors)
items.one_line: Lawyers, CAs and doctors in India may not solicit work or advertise themselves; their websites, posts and bios are limited to factual information, with no client names, success stories, 'best/leading' claims, testimonials or boasts of cures.

sources.supports: full text of BCI Rule 36; BCI directives of 08.07.2024 to enforce the ban on online platforms

sources.title: ICAI Advisory, 14 Oct 2020: Website Guidelines of the Institute (No. M-626/14/2020)
sources.supports: clauses (6) and (7) bar solicitation and advertisement; list of prohibited website contents

sources.title: Indian Medical Council (Professional Conduct, Etiquette and Ethics) Regulations, 2002 (West Bengal Consumer Affairs copy; NMC lists the same regulations at nmc.org.in)
sources.supports: reg 6.1 Advertising: soliciting unethical, no self-promotion, no endorsements of products, no boasting of cures; permitted formal announcements

sources.title: Medical Dialogues (secondary), Aug 2023: NMC puts RMP (Professional Conduct) Regulations 2023 on hold
sources.supports: 2023 regulations held in abeyance; 2002 regulations remain the operative code

items.note: Status read 2026-10-05: BCI Rule 36 (BCI Rules 1975) in force, reaffirmed by BCI directives of 08.07.2024 (PIB 2043470); ICAI Website Guidelines as revised Feb 2020 in force; for doctors the IMC 2002 regulations are operative because the NMC RMP (Professional Conduct) Regulations 2023 were notified 2 Aug 2023 and put in abeyance on 23 Aug 2023 (secondary sources; check nmc.org.in before quoting the 2023 social-media rules). Rules for a copywriter: (1) Advocates: 'An advocate shall not solicit work or advertise, either directly or indirectly, whether by circulars, advertisements, touts, personal communications ...' (the rule also names interviews, inspired newspaper comments and published photographs of their cases) (Rule 36 as quoted in PIB 2043470); the BCI has had State Bar Councils send cease-and-desist notices to online platforms listing lawyers. Write law-firm sites and LinkedIn posts as information and commentary, never 'hire us', case wins, client lists or ratings. (2) CAs: clauses (6) and (7) of Part I of the First Schedule to the CA Act 'bar solicitation and advertisement'; CA websites must not show client names or logos, fees or 'free' services, non-passport photos or event galleries, 'Leading Firm'/'Best Firm'/'Top Firm', claims of liaison with government offices, subjective claims such as 'best quality services in the market', awards, gradings, media coverage, or non-educational videos (ICAI Advisory 14 Oct 2020); breaching Council guidelines is itself professional misconduct. (3) Doctors: 'Soliciting of patients directly or indirectly, by a physician, by a group of physicians or by institutions or organisations is unethical'; no publicity that invites attention to the doctor's 'skill, qualification, achievements' or results in 'self aggrandizement'; no endorsement of any drug, appliance or commercial product; must not 'boast of cases, operations, cures or remedies'; formal press announcements are allowed only for starting practice, change of type of practice or address, temporary absence, resumption or succession, and public declaration of charges (IMC 2002 reg 6.1.1); own photo on letterhead or signboard counts as self-advertisement (6.1.2). Hospital and clinic ads also fall under comp:dmr_act_1954 and comp:asci_code.

items.name: Identity of victims of sexual offences and child victims in India: POCSO Act s.23, BNS s.72-73, Supreme Court (Nipun Saxena 2018) and Press Council norms
items.one_line: News, social and campaign copy about rape, sexual assault or child sexual abuse must never print the victim's name, photo or any detail (school, village, family, relative's face) that could identify them; a child's identity can be disclosed only on a Special Court's written permission.

sources.title: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (Gazette text, MHA copy)
sources.supports: s.72 (printing or publishing the victim's name or identifying matter, exceptions) and s.73 (court proceedings)

sources.title: Supreme Court, Nipun Saxena v. Union of India, 11 Dec 2018 (Indian Kanoon copy)
sources.supports: binding directions on not identifying victims 'even in a remote manner'; quotes POCSO s.23 in full; blurred-face example

sources.title: Press Council of India: Norms of Journalistic Conduct, 2022 edition
sources.supports: Caution against Identification; minors born of sexual abuse; privacy of minors in public figures' families; witnesses not to be identified

items.note: In force: BNS s.72 (replaced IPC s.228A from 1 July 2024), POCSO Act 2012 s.23, SC directions of 11 Dec 2018; PCI Norms 2022 edition (all read 2026-10-05). Rules for a copywriter: (1) printing or publishing 'the name or any matter which may make known the identity of any person against whom an offence' under BNS s.64-71 'is alleged or found to have been committed' is punishable (BNS s.72(1)); exceptions only for police in good faith for the investigation, the victim's own written authorisation, or next of kin's written authorisation (dead, child or unsound-mind victim) and then only to a recognised welfare organisation (s.72(2)). Publishing court proceedings in such cases needs the court's permission, though High Court and Supreme Court judgments may be published (s.73). (2) Child victims: 'No reports in any media shall disclose, the identity of a child including his name, address, photograph, family details, school, neighbourhood ...', unless the Special Court permits it in writing; and no report or comment on a child 'without having complete and authentic information' (POCSO s.23(1)-(2), as quoted by the SC); the publisher or owner is jointly liable for staff (s.23(3)). (3) no one may publish, in 'print, electronic, social media, etc.', 'the name of the victim or even in a remote manner disclose any facts which can lead to the victim being identified' (Nipun Saxena, direction 1). The court gave examples that still identify: a blurred face with relatives, neighbours or the village name visible, or 'she had topped the State Board Examination' with the state named. FIRs in these cases are not to be put in the public domain (direction 3). (4) PCI: 'the names, photographs of the victims or other particulars directly or indirectly leading to their identity shall not be published' when reporting rape, abduction or kidnap of women or sexual assault on children; children born of sexual abuse 'shall not be identified or photographed'; do not identify witnesses (Norms 2022, privacy section). (5) Practical: no names (not even first names or 'a 14-year-old from [named school]'), no photos or recreations that show the victim's face, home, school or family, no hashtags with the victim's name, even in outrage or justice-campaign posts. Use 'the survivor' or 'the child'.

items.name: Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities) Rules, 2011: mandatory declarations on packages and on e-commerce listings
items.one_line: Every pre-packaged product label, and every e-commerce listing for it, must carry the fixed declarations: maker / packer / importer, country of origin, generic name, net quantity, MRP inclusive of all taxes, unit sale price, consumer-care contact and dates.

sources.title: Department of Consumer Affairs: Book on Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities) Rules, 2011 with all amendments
sources.supports: consolidated rule 6 text incl. sub-rule (10) e-commerce (G.S.R. 629(E), 23 Jun 2017) and sub-rule (11) unit sale price (G.S.R. 226(E), w.e.f. 1 Oct 2022)

sources.title: PIB: Centre amends the Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities) Rules 2011 (Nov 2021)
sources.supports: press release on the 2021 amendment (not read in full)

items.note: In force; text read 2026-10-05 in the Department of Consumer Affairs consolidated book (latest amendment visible in it: G.S.R. 226(E) of 28 Mar 2022, w.e.f. 1 Oct 2022; the book carries no 'as of' date, so check for later amendments). For product-listing and packaging copy: (1) Every package must bear 'a definite, plain and conspicuous declaration' of: maker (and packer, or importer for imports); country of origin for imported products; common or generic name; net quantity in standard units; month and year of manufacture or pre-packing; retail sale price shown as maximum retail price 'inclusive of all taxes' (illustrations: 'MRP Rs. xx.xx incl. of all taxes'); size where relevant; 'best before' or 'use by' where applicable (r.6(1)). (2) Name, address, telephone number and e-mail of the person to contact 'in case of consumer complaints' (r.6(2)). (3) Unit sale price 'in rupees, rounded off to the nearest two decimal place' per gram/kg, ml/litre, cm/metre or per number, not needed where MRP equals unit price (r.6(11)). (4) E-commerce: 'the mandatory declarations ..., except the month and year in which the commodity is manufactured or packed, shall be displayed' on the e-commerce listing; on a marketplace, the seller / manufacturer / importer is responsible for their correctness if the platform only hosts the information (r.6(10)). So a product-page writer must include these fields, not only the marketing description. (5) Food packages follow FSSAI labelling instead for the maker declaration (r.6(1) Explanation III); see comp:fssai_advertising_claims_2018. Penalties under the Legal Metrology Act not quoted from memory.

items.name: Outbrain and Taboola (Realize) advertiser content policies for native / recommendation-widget ads: headlines, thumbnails, branding text, AI content
items.one_line: Native-widget ads on Outbrain and Taboola are rejected for headlines that mislead, exaggerate or sensationalise, all-caps or excessive punctuation, emoji in titles, before/after images, celebrities used for product endorsement, and source names that hide who the advertiser is.

sources.title: Outbrain: Advertising Guidelines (advertisers)
sources.supports: Headline and Source Guidelines; banned sensational words; capitalisation, punctuation, no emoji; source name; image rules; landing page; AI-generated content rules

sources.title: Taboola Realize Help: Title, Thumbnail and Branding Text Policies (dated August 31, 2026; redirects to realize.com)
sources.supports: title rules, thumbnail rules incl. before/after and celebrities, thumbnail minimum size, branding text

items.note: Both pages read 2026-10-05; Taboola's advertiser help now lives under its 'Realize' brand. Rules for a headline writer: (1) Outbrain prohibits 'Inaccurate, Misleading, or Overly Sensational Headlines', headlines that exaggerate or embellish the content, and '"Too good to be true" headlines (i.e. "One weird trick that will help you lose that belly fat")'; its content guidance tells writers to remove words such as 'stuns', 'reveals', 'real reason', 'last words', 'years later', 'you won't believe' and similar phrases. (2) Outbrain style: no excessive capitalisation ("LEARN MORE" is wrong; content-type labels like 'VIDEO:' and acronyms are fine), 'Always capitalize the first letter of the headline', correct grammar, no repeated or aggressive punctuation, and 'The use of emojis of any kind is prohibited in the titles'. (3) Taboola: 'Titles must not be misleading and must accurately reflect the subject of the landing page', 'must not be in all capital letters or contain excessive punctuation', must be correctly spelled and grammatical in the targeted territory's language, and 'must not contain solely the product price'. (4) Images: both ban before/after photos and celebrities or politicians for product endorsement (Taboola: unless you have documented permission); a celebrity named in a title must match the one in the image (Outbrain); Taboola thumbnails need minimum width 400px, minimum length 350px, max 5MB. (5) Disclosure and honesty: the source / branding text under the headline must accurately show who is behind the content; Outbrain bans fake testimonials, fake comments, fake earned-media logos and auto-refreshing date stamps on landing pages, and requires AI-generated or AI-modified ad content to be 'clearly labelled as AI-generated at the point of first exposure', with no synthetic likenesses or voice clones of real people without consent and disclosure. Related: comp:ftc_native_advertising, comp:asci_code, comp:india_personality_rights.

items.name: RBI Fair Practices Code and recovery-agent conduct for banks and NBFCs (now in the Responsible Business Conduct Directions, 2025)
items.one_line: Loan, EMI-reminder and collection messages from a bank, NBFC or their agents must be in a language the borrower understands, identify the agent, and never threaten, shame, spam on social media or call outside the permitted hours.

sources.title: RBI: Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 1, 2026)
sources.supports: title and update date read on rbi.org.in 2026-10-05; the PDF on rbidocs.rbi.org.in sits behind a CAPTCHA, so its recovery-agent rules (8:00 a.m.-7:00 p.m. calling window, no inappropriate social-media messages) are from a web-search summary only

sources.title: RBI: Master Circular - Fair Practices Code (NBFCs), 1 Jul 2015
sources.supports: vernacular-language communications, no harassment at odd hours (historic text, consolidated into the 2025 Directions)

sources.title: RBI: Recovery Agents engaged by banks, 24 Apr 2008
sources.supports: agent must carry the bank's notice, authorisation letter and identity card; training on hours of calling and privacy

sources.title: RBI/2022-23/108: Responsibilities of regulated entities employing recovery agents (Aug 2022)
sources.supports: origin of the 8 a.m.-7 p.m. calling restriction across commercial banks, co-operative banks, NBFCs, ARCs and AIFIs (behind CAPTCHA; known from search summary)

items.note: Status as read 2026-10-05: RBI consolidated its instructions into entity-wise Directions in 2025; the NBFC Responsible Business Conduct Directions, 2025 are 'Updated as on July 1, 2026' (rbi.org.in). The Directions' own PDF was behind a CAPTCHA (not bypassed), so rules (3)-(4) below are from older RBI texts plus a search summary: medium confidence; read the current Direction for your entity type (bank, NBFC, co-operative bank) before quoting. For a copywriter drafting collection SMS / WhatsApp / emails, call scripts or loan-offer copy: (1) 'All communications to the borrower shall be in the vernacular language or a language as understood by the borrower' (FPC Master Circular 2015, para 2A(i)(a)). (2) Lenders 'should not resort to undue harassment viz; persistently bothering the borrowers at odd hours, use muscle power for recovery of loans' (same, para on recovery). (3) Per RBI's 2022 circular and the 2025 Directions (search summary): no intimidation or harassment of any kind, verbal or physical, no acts 'intended to humiliate publicly' or intrude on the privacy of family members and friends, no inappropriate messages on mobile or social media, no threatening or anonymous calls, and no persistent calls before 8:00 a.m. or after 7:00 p.m. for overdue loans. (4) The borrower must be told which recovery agency is acting, and the agent carries 'the notice and the authorization letter from the bank along with the identity card' (2008 circular): collection messages should name the lender and the agency. Penalties not taken from memory. Related: comp:rbi_digital_lending_2025 (digital loan apps).

items.name: Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016: advertising a real-estate project (registration number, Authority website, carpet area, veracity) and state RERA orders
items.one_line: A builder's ad, brochure, hoarding or social post may run only for a RERA-registered project, must show the registration number and the RERA website prominently (Maharashtra also requires a QR code), and every claim in it is a promise the promoter compensates for if false.

sources.title: Indian Kanoon: Section 11 in the RERA Act, 2016
sources.supports: s.11(2) text: ad must mention Authority website and registration number (secondary; India Code PDF unreachable 2026-10-05)

sources.title: Lawsisto: The Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016 (full text)
sources.supports: s.2(b) advertisement, s.2(k) carpet area, s.3(1) no advertising before registration, s.12 compensation for false statements (secondary reproduction, read via fetch summary)

sources.title: MahaRERA: Suo Motu Advertisement Case No. 43 of 2024
sources.supports: quotes MahaRERA Order No. 46/2023 (29.05.2023) and 46A/2023 (25.07.2023): QR code beside registration number and website on every ad after 01.08.2023

sources.title: MahaRERA: Orders and Circulars
sources.supports: index of state orders incl. Order No. 46C/2025 on QR code and font size of the registration number (search listing; not read)

items.note: Act in force (central text read via secondary reproductions 2026-10-05, India Code unreachable: medium confidence); each state has its own RERA rules and authority orders. For a real-estate copywriter: (1) 'Advertisement' means 'any document described or issued as advertisement through any medium and includes any notice, circular or other documents or publicity in any form' (s.2(b)): brochures, hoardings, WhatsApp forwards, reels and listing pages all count. (2) 'No promoter shall advertise, market, book, sell or offer for sale, or invite persons to purchase in any manner' a plot, apartment or building in a project that needs registration without registering it (s.3(1)): no 'pre-launch' or 'EOI' teasers before registration. (3) 'The advertisement or prospectus ... shall mention prominently the website address of the Authority ... and include the registration number obtained from the Authority' (s.11(2)). (4) Area claims: the Act defines 'carpet area' as 'the net usable floor area of an apartment, excluding ... external walls, ... services shafts, exclusive balcony or verandah area and exclusive open terrace area' (s.2(k)); quote sizes as carpet area, not an inflated super built-up figure. (5) A buyer who pays on the basis of the ad and suffers loss 'by reason of any incorrect, false statement included therein' must be compensated by the promoter (s.12): amenities, possession dates and approvals in copy must match the registered project. State pattern (Maharashtra): 'The Promoter shall prominently display QR Code on each and every project promotion/advertisement published after 01.08.2023' beside the MahaRERA registration number and website address (MahaRERA Order 46/2023 as quoted in Case 43 of 2024); MahaRERA has since issued Order 46C/2025 on QR and font size (not read). Check the project's own state RERA orders before finalising. Penalties not taken from memory.

items.name: Representation of the People Act, 1951 section 123: corrupt practices (religion / caste appeals, promoting enmity, false statements about candidates)
items.one_line: Election slogans, speeches, ads and posts for a candidate may not appeal for votes on religion, race, caste, community or language, use religious or national symbols, stoke enmity between groups, or publish false statements of fact about a rival's character.

sources.title: Indian Kanoon: Section 123 in The Representation of the People Act, 1951
sources.supports: current text of s.123 clauses (1)-(8): bribery, undue influence, appeals on religion etc., enmity, sati, false statements (secondary reproduction; India Code refused fetch 2026-10-05)

items.note: In force (statute text read on Indian Kanoon 2026-10-05; India Code refused the fetch, so medium confidence). Applies to the candidate, the agent, or 'any other person with the consent of a candidate or his election agent', which covers the agency or writer producing campaign copy. Rules for a political copywriter: (1) No appeal 'to vote or refrain from voting for any person on the ground of his religion, race, caste, community or language', and no use of or appeal to religious symbols or 'national symbols, such as the national flag or the national emblem' to further a candidate's prospects; the party symbol allotted under the Act is not a religious or national symbol for this purpose (s.123(3)). (2) No 'promotion of, or attempt to promote, feelings of enmity or hatred between different classes ... on grounds of religion, race, caste, community, or language' (s.123(3A)). (3) No publication 'of any statement of fact which is false', believed false or not believed true, about 'the personal character or conduct of any candidate' or about anyone's candidature or withdrawal, reasonably calculated to hurt their prospects (s.123(4)): satire and opinion are safer than invented facts. (4) Threatening voters with 'divine displeasure or spiritual censure' is undue influence, but 'a declaration of public policy, or a promise of public action' is not (s.123(2)). (5) Bribery covers any gratification to an elector, including entertainment (s.123(1)): giveaway or contest copy tied to voting is out. A proven corrupt practice can void an election; consequences not quoted from memory. Pair with comp:eci_mcc (Model Code) and comp:rpa_s127a_election_print.

items.name: SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015: material-event disclosure (Reg 30), annual report MD&A and BRSR
items.one_line: A listed company must tell the stock exchanges first, within fixed hours, about material events, and everything it disseminates (press release, shareholder letter, annual report) must be accurate, not misleading and in simple language.

sources.title: SEBI: LODR Regulations, 2015 [Last amended on July 14, 2026]
sources.supports: official consolidated text page; PDF https://www.sebi.gov.in/sebi_data/attachdocs/jul-2026/1784630770711.pdf read 2026-10-05

sources.title: SEBI: FAQs for LODR Regulations (Apr 2025)
sources.supports: SEBI's own FAQ on the regulations (not read in full)

items.note: In force; consolidated text 'Amended up to July 14, 2026' (SEBI PDF, read 2026-10-05). For a copywriter writing IR / PR copy for a listed company: (1) Principles: the entity 'shall refrain from misrepresentation and ensure that the information provided to recognised stock exchange(s) and investors is not misleading', and disseminations must be 'adequate, accurate, explicit, timely and presented in a simple language' (Reg 4). (2) Exchange first: material events/information go to the stock exchange(s) FIRST, within 30 minutes of the board meeting closing (3 hours if it closes after market hours), 12 hours if the event emanates from within the company, 24 hours if from outside; a late disclosure must carry an explanation for the delay (Reg 30(6)). So a press release, social post or shareholder letter about a material event must not go out before the exchange filing. (3) The same events are put on the company website (Reg 30(8)). (4) Top 100, then top 250, listed entities must confirm, deny or clarify a specific mainstream-media rumour within 24 hours of a material price movement; if confirming, give the current stage (Reg 30(11)). (5) Annual report contents include a Management Discussion and Analysis report (industry structure, opportunities and threats, segment performance, outlook, risks and concerns, internal controls, financial vs operational performance, HR developments: Schedule V Part B) and, for the top 1,000 listed entities by market cap, a Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report (Reg 34(2)(f)). Penalties not taken from memory.

items.name: SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015: UPSI, fair-disclosure code and trading window
items.one_line: Unpublished price-sensitive information about a listed company may not be leaked, teased or selectively shared in IR, PR or social copy; it must be released uniformly to everyone at once.

sources.title: SEBI: PIT Regulations, 2015 [Last amended on March 12, 2025]
sources.supports: official consolidated text page; PDF https://www.sebi.gov.in/sebi_data/attachdocs/aug-2026/1786963663321.pdf ('Amended upto March 12, 2025', includes amendments w.e.f. June 10, 2025) read 2026-10-05

sources.title: SEBI: Comprehensive FAQs on PIT Regulations (Apr 2025)
sources.supports: SEBI's own FAQ (not read in full)

items.note: In force; SEBI consolidated text 'Amended upto March 12, 2025' with 2025 amendments effective June 10, 2025 (read 2026-10-05). For IR / PR / social copy: (1) UPSI = information 'not generally available which upon becoming generally available, is likely to materially affect the price', ordinarily including financial results, dividends, capital-structure changes, M&A and big contract wins or losses outside the normal course, KMP changes, rating changes, fund raising, fraud or defaults (Reg 2(1)(n)). Never hint at these in a teaser, 'big news coming' post, interview or analyst deck before the exchange disclosure. (2) 'No insider shall communicate, provide, or allow access to any unpublished price sensitive information' except for 'legitimate purposes, performance of duties or discharge of legal obligations' (Reg 3(1)); agencies and writers who get drafts are handled on a need-to-know basis. (3) 'Generally available information' is information accessible on a non-discriminatory basis and 'shall not include unverified event or information reported in print or electronic media' (Reg 2(1)(e)): a news leak does not make it public. (4) Fair-disclosure principles: prompt public disclosure, 'Uniform and universal dissemination ... to avoid selective disclosure', information shared with analysts must not be UPSI, and transcripts or records of analyst / IR meetings go on the official website (Schedule A). (5) The trading window for designated persons is closed from the end of every quarter till 48 hours after results (Schedule B); results-season copy and quotes from insiders are drafted inside that quiet period, so drafts stay need-to-know. Penalties not taken from memory.

items.name: Uniform Code for Pharmaceutical Marketing Practices (UCPMP) 2024: what drug promotion and medical-detailing copy may claim
items.one_line: Pharma promotion to doctors may start only after marketing approval, must be balanced and substantiable, may not call a drug 'safe' without qualification or 'new' after a year, and must carry the prescribing basics.

sources.title: UCPMP 2024 (Department of Pharmaceuticals, dated 12th March 2024), copy hosted by Novo Nordisk India
sources.supports: full code text: general points, claims and comparisons, promotional material, brand reminders (company-hosted copy of the government code; pharmaceuticals.gov.in not fetched)

sources.title: Cyril Amarchand Mangaldas: FAQs on UCPMP 2024 (Mar 2024)
sources.supports: secondary law-firm commentary (not read in full)

items.note: UCPMP 2024 issued by the Department of Pharmaceuticals, dated 12 March 2024 (text read 2026-10-05 in a company-hosted copy: medium-high confidence). A drug's marketing approval itself comes from CDSCO under the New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules, 2019 (not read in this pass). For medical writers and pharma copywriters: (1) 'a drug must not be promoted prior to receipt of its marketing approval', and promotion 'must be consistent with the terms of its marketing approval' (1.2): no off-label indications. (2) Information 'must be balanced, up-to-date, verifiable, must not mislead either directly or by implication' and 'must be capable of substantiation' on request (1.3). (3) 'The word "safe" must not be used without qualification', no categorical 'no side effects' claims; 'The word "new" must not be used' for a drug generally available or promoted in India for more than a year (2.2-2.3). (4) Comparisons must be factual, fair and substantiable; no competitor brand names without their prior consent; no disparaging other companies or doctors' opinions (2.4-2.7). (5) Promotional material for prescribers must include the authorisation holder's name and address, the generic names of active ingredients adjacent to the brand name, dosage and method of use, adverse reactions, warnings, precautions and contraindications, and the date the particulars were last updated (3.2); paid journal pieces must not resemble editorial matter (3.3); no names or photographs of healthcare professionals (3.6); exposed mailings must not carry matter that reads as advertising to the lay public (3.9). Public-facing cure claims fall under comp:dmr_act_1954. Penalties and enforcement not quoted from memory.

items.name: YouTube Spam Policy (malicious clickbait, misleading metadata and thumbnails, scams, engagement manipulation, mass-produced AI content)
items.one_line: YouTube bans titles, thumbnails and descriptions that promise what the video does not deliver, scam and get-rich-quick pitches, engagement bait, comment spam, scraped re-uploads and mass-produced repetitive AI videos; strikes and demonetisation follow.
aliases: YouTube spam deceptive practices and scams policy

sources.title: YouTube Help: Spam Policy (formerly 'Spam, deceptive practices, and scams policies')
sources.supports: full current policy: scope incl. titles, thumbnails, links, comments; examples for each violation type; enforcement (warning, strikes, termination, monetisation)

items.note: Current page read 2026-10-05; it is now titled 'Spam Policy' and sits beside separate Impersonation, External links and Fake engagement policies. Rules for a copywriter: (1) It covers metadata, not just video: 'This policy applies to all types of content on YouTube, including unlisted and private content, comments, links, posts and thumbnails'. (2) Malicious clickbait = 'Using maliciously misleading titles, thumbnails, descriptions, or imagery to trick users into clicking on a video that does not deliver what was promised' (example: a title offering a full sports match when the video is a clip). A curiosity title is fine; a title the video does not pay off is not. (3) 'It's okay to ask viewers to like, comment, or subscribe', but not to offer rewards for likes, views or subscribers, run sub-for-sub schemes, or post 'high volumes of low-effort, repetitive polls'. (4) No scam copy: 'get rich quick' investment schemes, fake job offers, fake customer-support numbers; no videos 'created solely to drive users off of YouTube'. (5) 'Automated or synthetic mass-production' is banned: using AI 'to churn out high volumes of similar content with minimal changes' (example: same music and AI imagery with an AI-read script across many videos); re-uploads need 'original commentary, educational value, or unique editing'. Enforcement: removal, warning then strikes ('3 strikes within 90 days' can terminate the channel), suspended monetisation. See comp:youtube_altered_synthetic and comp:youtube_paid_promotion.
